rv.q: Further, you may have been part of the cult yourself. Did you throw toast at a midnight screening? Did you scream choreographed insults — pretty vile ones, now that I think about it — whenever the actors said "Brad" or "Janet"?

Roundabout Theatre Company's exuberant Broadway revival of the show, directed by Sam Pinkleton and featuring a killer cast led by international heartthrob Luke Evans as Frank, makes roughly the same invitation. It's an awfully hard one to resist.

Ideally a show charging hundreds of dollars a seat would make things more legible than Pinkleton has, to best ensure that everyone is having a good time, not just those who have heard these lines, and said their own, countless times before.

Pinkleton, so masterful with 'Oh, Mary!,' just didn't catch the right vocabulary for 'Rocky Horror,' a deceptively tough assignment on a show popping up again to remind us of just how easily people were shocked in the 1970s. O'Brien's cultural legacy is not as trivial as you might think.

The production will no doubt satisfy 'Rocky Horror Show' fetishists who still find comfort in the liturgical rituals of a by-gone counter-culture. Others, however, will just find themselves in a tired time warp.

It's a tricky spot taking on such an iconic role originally played to perfection by Curry, but this is no mere shadow cast performance. Evans manages to capture the character's scintillating combination of dangerous sexuality and emotional vulnerability, all while adding his own devilish spin.

With immensely appealing performances from Luke Evans (yes, he most certainly can sing) as the sinister Frank-N-Furter, Rachel Dratch as the droll narrator, this Roundabout-produced Rocky Horror revival is a first-rate presentation of a property that, along with John Waters' early work, pretty much defined a certain strain of '70s counter-cultur...

The halls of Studio 54 should be proud with the glittery whirlwind happening on stage eight times a week. It's Sam Pinkleton to a tee, and boy is it fun. It's a type of revival that will please the fans and welcome newcomers to the world justly. Head over to the lab, and keep dreaming.

There are no shortage of lush performances and lavish production design. Supporting performers like Michaela Jaé Rodriguez (as Columbia), Harvey Guillén (doubling as Eddie and Dr. Scott), and Josh Rivera (as Rocky) round out a strong cast, and each have their moments to shine. There are almost too many places to look.
If this all sounds appealing to you as it certainly is to me, then head on out to Studio 54.

This Rocky Horror is not without flaws, but it hardly matters. The style carries you along, and the energy rarely falters. For nearly two hours, it delivers what it promises: a weird, exuberant, and thoroughly enjoyable night out. Participation optional, temptation unavoidable.

The rather patronizing announcement works, and the sexily performed, well-sung production from “Oh, Mary!” director Sam Pinkleton for the most part reverts back to the 1973 musical’s quieter origins before superfans in fishnets began shouting back at the screen and throwing rice at midnight movie screenings down in the Village.

For the record, it is by far the most lavish production of the show ever to play Broadway. All those visual accoutrements help to deliver Rachel Dratch's absolutely riveting narrator, a vast improvement on Dick Cavett's from the 2000. Broadway revival.

Solidly produced, this revival still feels like a missed opportunity to be the wild must-attend event of the season. It's Rocky Horror at Studio 54 for crying out loud. If we can't let loose here, where can we?

But this history of audience involvement – not just interaction but parallel creation – is surely the main reason this show is still around. One can still enjoy The Rocky Horror Show, especially Richard O'Brien's 15 songs, most of which are catchy. But its shock value has largely worn off, and, let's be honest, without that, what is there?

This starry production leans fully into the show's campy pleasures, delivering plenty of laughs, strong performances and visual flair. But it rarely taps into the provocative, more unpredictable undercurrent that gives Rocky Horror its countercultural bite. And without that sense of risk, much of the evening feels curiously weightless.

The morning after witnessing the new Broadway staging of The Rocky Horror Show at Studio 54, it's difficult to recall much to remark upon. So I guess this revival cannot be considered, at least by me, a memorable production from the Roundabout Theatre Company.

The original live stage version, sans Picture, has been exhumed in revival under the Roundabout aegis. And on the evidence, it's time to bid the sucker farewell, particularly as staged here: large, loud, and expensive in a setting utterly unsuited to it.

Lord knows we need more subversion. In a season of blah musicals squeezed out of mid movies or TV (Beaches, Schmigadoon!, The Lost Boys), Rocky Horror stands out as a trash masterpiece that knows what you want and intends to give it to you, hard.

The net effect feels like its full of invention yet perhaps trying too hard, though the sexual scenes (including a quick glimpse of male-on-male ass play) manage to be compelling and hilarious at once. Hot patootie, bless my soul!

Varying degrees of stage experience among the cast give an adult-learner college production vibe as glaring as the neon green rope lights strung throughout the theater. Nostalgic, sure, but is this the caliber Broadway audiences expect to see? If only there were a post-show cast party at Denny's.

Evans makes a striking impression as Frank — towering over the cast in his four-inch heels while delivering a performance that is in turns seductive, off-putting, and out of this world. And Frank really does seem sweet — not the walking provocateur that Tim Curry embodied a half century ago.
Looks aren't everything. A first-rate Rocky Horror should make one feel like, pardon the expression, a hot patootie. This version too often seems just warmed-over.

sg.vl: Center Orchestra front-to-mid is the house sweet spot
sg.ra: SeatPlan and TickPick both identify center Orchestra Rows A-E as offering the most direct, immersive sightlines. The stage's setback (per TickPick) enhances Row A viewing, and Rows F-H avoid the Front Mezzanine overhang that begins at Row M. Headout lists 15 orchestra rows (A-P) totaling ~521-538 seats depending on source.

SeatPlan explicitly flags Rows F-H as 'good value seats' that avoid Front Mezzanine overhang disruption and sit at a comfortable distance from the stage. Headout and TickPick echo the value framing for this band. Pricing typically below the Row A-E premium band.

SeatPlan describes Center Front Mezz AA-BB as 'very popular' with 'excellently raked seats and expansive overhead sightlines.' No Rear Mezz overhang exists above this section. Headout prices most Center Front Mezz seats around $224. Row AA safety rail can clip the stage for shorter patrons, so Row BB is the refined pick.

SeatPlan: Left-section Front Mezz has 'more restricted sightlines of action at the corner of stage right'; Right section mirrors this toward stage left. Legroom described as 'particularly cramped' at side seats. Still elevated with no overhang above, so sightlines to center stage remain workable.

SeatPlan calls 'rows FF and GG in the Center Rear Mezzanine' the Rear Mezz sweet spot; Headout flags EE-GG as good value ('a good look at the stage without costing as much'). Row EE sits directly behind a horizontal aisle per the SeatPlan overview. Steep rake trades legroom for sightlines.

sg.vl: Side-angle obstruction into opposite stage half
sg.ra: SeatPlan and TickPick both warn that Left Rear Mezz Rows HH-NN have obstructed sightlines into stage right, and Right Rear Mezz mirrors this to stage left. Combined with the steep rake, tight legroom, and distance, these rows deliver the weakest experience in the house.

vr.q: it feels a little bit soulless... it has become one of those tours like a Blood Brothers that just goes round and round and round
